title: Am I my brother's keeper (Genesis 4:1–16)
hookLine: Cain kills Abel and God still puts a mark of protection on him

lines: IT'S A LIE, TOLD TO GOD.
cards: A line from Genesis gets quoted far from Genesis. A politician uses it in a speech. A teacher writes it on a board.
Someone mutters it when asked to help a neighbor: what am I, my brother's keeper? It sounds like a shrug. In Genesis, it's a lie, told to God's face, by a man who has just killed his brother.
Two brothers, born outside Eden. One works the soil, one keeps sheep. They both bring an offering.
And one of them doesn't come home.

teach.h: WHY ABEL'S? THE TEXT IS SILENT.
teach.b: First, the offerings. Cain brings fruit of the ground; Abel brings the firstlings of his flock. God has respect to Abel's offering and not to Cain's.
Why? Genesis is silent, and readers have offered guesses; the Letter to the Hebrews says Abel offered by faith. Second, the warning.
Cain's face falls, and God speaks to him before anything happens: sin lies at the door, but you can master it. Cain doesn't answer. He takes his brother into the field and kills him.
Third, the question. As in the garden, God asks what God already knows. In the Douay-Rheims: "Where is thy brother Abel? And he answered, I know not: am I my brother's keeper?"
Adam hid. Cain lies, then shrugs.
And God says: "The voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me from the earth." The ground that took Adam's sweat now drinks a brother's blood.
The Catechism quotes this scene when it teaches the sacredness of every human life. Fourth, the surprise.
Cain is sent out as a wanderer, afraid someone will kill him, and God puts a mark on him: not a brand of shame, but a sign of protection.
Nobody is to take his life. Even for a murderer, God keeps the door open. Catholics remember Abel at the altar: the Roman Canon names the offering of Abel the just.
Genesis leaves Cain's question hanging. Readers hear the rest of scripture answer it: yes.

how: In the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer, the priest asks God to accept the offering as he accepted the gifts of Abel the just, the sacrifice of Abraham and the offering of Melchizedek.

games.q: you're Cain. you've just come back from the field alone. God asks: where is thy brother Abel? what do you say?
o: I know not: am I my brother's keeper?
he went to tend the sheep.
games.why: Cain lies, then shrugs. and God answers: the voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me from the earth.

practice: Let the face of a brother or sister come to mind, by blood or someone who's been one to you, and ask where they are this week and what's hard for them right now.
If there's distance between you, notice it without blaming anyone, and just hold them. If you pray, pray for them by name.
